_note: Sensitosis test bank. sens/spec: v = figure used for the reveal, lo/hi = range that scores full marks (CI or spread across studies). spec null = no good source, sensitivity-only round. kind: sign (Physical sign), rule (Clinical rule), scan (Scan), missing = Lab test; sign and rule rounds show as Signs rounds; label overrides the chip text. Every figure was read from the linked source(s); lab tests checked 1 Nov 2026, physical signs and clinical rules checked 2 Nov 2026.

rat-sym.scenario: Sore throat, runny nose, feeling rubbish. You swab yourself at home.
rat-sym.says: Great at false alarms (it barely makes any). Less great at catching COVID: about 1 in 4 people with symptoms test negative. A negative RAT with symptoms is worth repeating.
rat-sym.note: Pooled across many brands and 109 evaluations in people with symptoms.
src: Cochrane review (Dinnes 2022), summarised in American Family Physician 2023

rat-asym.scenario: You feel perfectly fine. You swab before visiting your nan, just in case.
rat-asym.says: Without symptoms, a RAT catches only about half of infections. A negative is reassuring-ish, not a free pass. A positive, though? Believe it.
rat-asym.note: Same Cochrane review. Fewer studies in people without symptoms (50 evaluations).
src: Cochrane review (Dinnes 2022), summarised in American Family Physician 2023

strep.scenario: A child with a sore throat gets a quick throat swab at the clinic. Result in minutes.
strep.says: Pretty good both ways. It misses about 1 in 7 strep throats, so a negative doesn’t fully rule it out.
strep.note: Children only. Results varied between brands and studies.
src: Cochrane review: rapid tests for strep throat in children (2016)

fit.scenario: The bowel screening kit arrives in the mail. You do the poo stick thing and post it back.
fit.says: Catches about 4 in 5 bowel cancers from one simple sample, and most people without cancer get a clear result. One reason the kit comes back every two years.
fit.note: Figures are for cancer, from a 2014 meta-analysis. They vary with the brand and the cut-off used.
src: Lee 2014 meta-analysis (Ann Intern Med), summarised in American Family Physician

ottawa.scenario: You rolled your ankle. The doctor presses a few bony spots and asks you to walk four steps. ‘Positive’ means: get an X-ray.
ottawa.says: A champion rule-out tool. It almost never misses a fracture, but most people it sends for an X-ray are fine. That’s the deal: it still cuts X-rays by about a third.
ottawa.note: Specificity varied a lot between studies.
src: Bachmann 2003 systematic review (BMJ), summarised in American Family Physician

psa4.test: PSA blood test (above 4 counts as high)
psa4.scenario: In a big US study, men had a prostate biopsy whatever their PSA was. A PSA above 4 counted as positive.
psa4.says: Ouch. At this cut-off, PSA missed about 4 in 5 of the cancers found on biopsy. No PSA level is both sensitive and specific.
psa4.note: From the Prostate Cancer Prevention Trial placebo group (Thompson 2005). Lower cut-offs catch more cancers but cause more false alarms.
src: Thompson 2005 (JAMA), abstract via US National Cancer Institute EDRN

psa3.test: PSA blood test (above 3 counts as high)
psa3.scenario: Same big US study, everyone biopsied. This time a PSA above 3 counts as positive.
psa3.says: Lower the bar and you catch more cancers (about 1 in 3), but false alarms jump too. Every cut-off is a trade.
psa3.note: Prostate Cancer Prevention Trial placebo group (Thompson 2005).
src: Thompson 2005 (JAMA), abstract via US National Cancer Institute EDRN

ddimer.scenario: Swollen calf after a long flight. Your risk looks low, so the doctor orders a D-dimer to rule out a clot.
ddimer.says: The classic rule-out test. Negative? A clot is very unlikely. Positive? Means little on its own: pregnancy, cancer, surgery, injury and inflammation all raise it.
ddimer.note: Older pooled data for lab (ELISA) assays; specificity was about 35 to 54% depending on the assay. Only useful when your risk is low to moderate.
src: Bounameaux 1997 review (QJM): pooled D-dimer accuracy by assay

mammo.scenario: A routine screening mammogram, no lumps, no symptoms. Just your two-yearly squish.
mammo.says: Catches most cancers, but because so few people being screened have cancer, most call-backs turn out fine. A call-back is not a diagnosis.
mammo.note: US data, 2007 to 2013, 1.6 million screens. Programs and countries differ.
src: Breast Cancer Surveillance Consortium (US) screening benchmarks

ferr30.scenario: Tired all the time. Your GP checks ferritin, your iron stores. Under 30 counts as positive.
ferr30.says: A cut-off of 30 catches most iron deficiency. The catch: inflammation pushes ferritin up, so it can look normal when it isn’t.
ferr30.note: Small studies that varied a lot. Experts say better studies are urgently needed.
src: Daru 2017 review: Serum ferritin as an indicator of iron status (Am J Clin Nutr)

ferr15.scenario: Same blood test, stricter cut-off: only a ferritin under 15 counts as low.
ferr15.says: Under 15, you can be pretty sure it’s iron deficiency. But this cut-off misses about a third of people who have it.
ferr15.note: Small, older studies with wide variation (one in pregnant women found much lower sensitivity).
src: Daru 2017 review: Serum ferritin as an indicator of iron status (Am J Clin Nutr)

trop99.scenario: Chest pain in the emergency department. One high-sensitivity troponin on arrival, usual cut-off.
trop99.says: One test too early misses about 1 in 10 heart attacks, because troponin takes time to rise. That’s why you get a second test.
trop99.note: Roche high-sensitivity troponin T at the 99th percentile. Another brand (Abbott troponin I) was the other way round: 75% sensitive, 94% specific.
src: NICE DG40: high-sensitivity troponin tests, evidence

trop01.test: Troponin, two tests an hour apart
trop01.scenario: Chest pain in ED. Troponin on arrival and again an hour later. ‘Negative’ means: ruled out.
trop01.says: Two tests an hour apart miss about 1 heart attack in 100. Not ruled out doesn’t mean you’re having one, just that you stay for more tests.
trop01.note: European 0/1-hour rule-out pathway. Specificity was 68% for one brand and 57% for another.
src: NICE DG40: high-sensitivity troponin tests, evidence

kernig.scenario: Fever and headache. The doctor bends your hip and knee, then straightens the knee. Pain or resistance is positive.
kernig.says: Famous, and nearly useless for ruling out. It missed 19 in 20 cases. A negative Kernig’s means nothing; worry anyway.
kernig.note: One study of 297 adults with suspected meningitis (Thomas 2002). Brudzinski’s sign did no better.
src: Thomas 2002 (Clin Infect Dis), summarised in American Family Physician

neck.scenario: Same fever and headache. This time the doctor checks whether your neck is stiff.
neck.says: The textbook sign caught fewer than 1 in 3 cases, and plenty of people without meningitis had it too. Classic doesn’t mean reliable.
src: Thomas 2002 (Clin Infect Dis), summarised in American Family Physician

fluA.scenario: Fever, aches, the works. A quick nose swab for influenza at the clinic.
fluA.says: A coin toss for catching flu in adults, but a positive is very believable. Good for ruling in, bad for ruling out.
fluA.note: Rapid antigen tests, meta-analysis 2012. Specificity was reported for all ages combined.
src: Chartrand 2012 meta-analysis (Ann Intern Med), summarised by ACP

fluK.scenario: A feverish, miserable kid. Quick nose swab for influenza.
fluK.says: Better in kids than in adults, but it still misses about 1 in 3.
fluK.note: Meta-analysis 2012. Specificity was reported for all ages combined.
src: Chartrand 2012 meta-analysis (Ann Intern Med), summarised by ACP

preg.scenario: Period’s late. You wee on the stick at home. Older studies watched real people do it.
preg.says: Trained volunteers caught about 9 in 10 pregnancies, but real people at home missed about 1 in 4. Testing too early is a big reason: if it’s negative and your period still hasn’t come, test again in a few days.
preg.note: Old studies (1972 to 1993); modern tests may do better. No good pooled figure for false positives, so this round has one slider.
src: Cole 2004 study, summarised in American Family Physician

calpro.scenario: Months of tummy pain and loose poo. IBS, or inflamed bowel? A poo test for calprotectin.
calpro.says: One of the good ones in adults. Negative? Inflamed bowel is unlikely, and you may skip a colonoscopy.
calpro.note: Meta-analysis of 6 adult studies (2010). Specificity varied a lot between studies.

calproK.scenario: A teenager with tummy pain, loose poo and weight loss. Same poo test.
calproK.says: Just as good at catching it in kids, but more false alarms: about 1 in 4 without bowel disease test positive.
calproK.note: Meta-analysis of 7 studies in children and teenagers (2010).

ubt.scenario: Burning tummy. You drink a special drink, then blow into a bag.
ubt.says: The best non-invasive test for H. pylori. Stop acid tablets and antibiotics beforehand or you’ll fool it.
ubt.note: The Cochrane review compared tests at a fixed specificity of about 90%, so that figure is set, not measured.
src: Cochrane review: non-invasive tests for H. pylori (2018)

hpstool.scenario: Same burning tummy, but this time it’s a poo sample instead of a breath test.
hpstool.says: Decent, cheap and easy, but a bit less sensitive than the breath test.
hpstool.note: Cochrane compared tests at a fixed specificity of about 90%.
src: Cochrane review: non-invasive tests for H. pylori (2018)

nitrite.scenario: Burning when you wee. The GP dips a strip in your urine. Positive here means the nitrite pad changes colour.
nitrite.says: Nitrite positive is a decent clue. Nitrite negative? Means little: about half of UTIs don’t show it.
nitrite.note: Pooled from 6 general practice studies (2004 meta-analysis).
src: Devillé 2004 meta-analysis: the urine dipstick test (BMC Urology)

dipany.test: Urine dipstick: nitrite or white cells
dipany.scenario: Same strip, but now either pad (nitrite or white cells) changing colour counts as positive.
dipany.says: Count either pad and you catch most UTIs, but you also get lots of false alarms. Symptoms still matter most.
dipany.note: General practice estimate rests on only 2 studies; treat as rough.
src: Devillé 2004 meta-analysis: the urine dipstick test (BMC Urology)

hpv.scenario: Routine cervical screening. The sample is tested for HPV, the virus behind almost all cervical cancer.
hpv.says: Much better at catching pre-cancer than the old Pap smear, which is why Australia switched to it in 2017.
hpv.note: Cochrane 2017, for moderate pre-cancer (CIN2+) using one HPV test (HC2). Figures differ slightly between tables in the review.
src: Cochrane review: cytology versus HPV testing (2017)

pap.scenario: The old way: cells smeared on a slide and checked under a microscope.
pap.says: Few false alarms, but it missed about 1 in 3 pre-cancers. Regular repeats made up for it, until the HPV test came along.
pap.note: Conventional cytology, abnormal cells of any grade counted as positive (Cochrane 2017).
src: Cochrane review: cytology versus HPV testing (2017)

mono.scenario: A teen with a wrecked throat, swollen glands and exhaustion. Quick blood test for glandular fever.
mono.says: Not bad, but early on it can miss up to 1 in 4 adults, and it’s poor in kids under 5. Too early? Test again later.
mono.note: From a systematic review; the authors say these figures probably flatter it in everyday practice.
src: Infectious mononucleosis: rapid evidence review (American Family Physician 2023)

crp.scenario: Chesty cough and fever. Could one CRP tell pneumonia from a plain chest infection?
crp.says: Studies were all over the place: sensitivity anywhere from 10 to 98%. So almost any guess scores today. That’s not a compliment to CRP.
crp.note: A 2005 systematic review found study quality generally poor and said CRP alone can’t rule pneumonia in or out. The grid shows the middle of the range.

usapp.scenario: A child with pain low on the right of the tummy. An ultrasound first, no radiation.
usapp.says: Very good in skilled hands, and no radiation. It misses about 1 in 8, so a doubtful scan gets a rethink.

ctapp.scenario: Same child, same pain, but this time a CT scan.
ctapp.says: A bit better than ultrasound, at the cost of radiation. One reason kids usually get ultrasound first.

dermo.scenario: A doctor checks a dark mole in person, looking through a dermatoscope (a lit magnifier).
dermo.says: The magnifier helps a lot: at the same false-alarm rate, it catches about 92 in 100 melanomas versus 76 by eye.
dermo.note: Cochrane 2018 compared methods at a fixed 80% specificity, so that figure is set, not measured. The review calls these figures illustrative.
src: Cochrane review: dermoscopy for diagnosing melanoma (2018)
dermo.label: Skin check

eye.scenario: Same mole, same doctor, but no dermatoscope: just a good look.
eye.says: By eye alone, about 1 in 4 melanomas slip past (at the same false-alarm rate). Get the magnifier out.
eye.note: Cochrane 2018 compared methods at a fixed 80% specificity. The review calls these figures illustrative.
src: Cochrane review: dermoscopy for diagnosing melanoma (2018)
eye.label: Skin check

brudz.scenario: Fever and a pounding headache. You lie flat and the doctor lifts your head towards your chest. If your hips and knees bend up by themselves, that’s positive.
brudz.says: Kernig’s famous sibling, and just as useless for ruling out: it caught 1 in 20 cases. A negative Brudzinski’s should reassure nobody.
brudz.note: One study of 297 adults with suspected meningitis (Thomas 2002). Kernig’s sign scored exactly the same.
src: Thomas 2002 (Clin Infect Dis), summarised in American Family Physician

jolt.scenario: Fever and headache. You shake your head side to side, two or three times a second. If the headache gets worse, that’s positive.
jolt.says: Once hyped as a near-perfect rule-out. A bigger review says it misses about 1 in 3. Head-shaking is not a substitute for a lumbar puncture.
jolt.note: Cochrane 2020: 9 studies, 1,161 people, very low certainty (hence the wide ranges). In people who were fully alert it caught about 75 in 100 and cleared about 61.
src: Cochrane review: jolt accentuation for meningitis (2020)

lachman.condition: a torn ACL (a key knee ligament)
lachman.scenario: You twisted your knee at netball and felt a pop. The doctor bends your knee slightly and tugs your shin forward to feel how far it slides.
lachman.says: One of the better bedside tests in all of medicine. It catches most torn ACLs and rarely cries wolf.
lachman.note: Pooled figures from the Benjaminse 2006 meta-analysis.

drawer.scenario: An old knee injury that keeps giving way. You lie with your knee bent to a right angle and the doctor pulls your shin forward, like opening a drawer.
drawer.says: Excellent for an old tear like this one. The same review found it far less reliable straight after an injury, when pain and swelling get in the way.
drawer.note: Benjaminse 2006 meta-analysis. These figures are for long-standing (chronic) tears only; it gave no good figures for fresh injuries.

mcmurray.scenario: Knee pain and clicking after a twist. The doctor bends your knee right up, twists the foot and straightens the leg, feeling for a painful click.
mcmurray.says: A coin toss with ambitions. It misses about 4 in 10 tears, and a click on its own proves nothing.
mcmurray.note: Smith 2015 meta-analysis: 9 studies, 1,234 people. An earlier review (Hegedus 2007) found 70 caught and 71 cleared, inside these ranges.

slr.scenario: Back pain shooting down one leg. You lie flat and the doctor slowly lifts your straight leg. If that brings on the pain down your leg, it’s positive.
slr.says: Brilliant at catching it, hopeless at clearing it: lots of people without a slipped disc get leg pain too. A negative test is the useful one. Lifting the other leg flips it: 28 caught, 90 cleared.
slr.note: Cochrane 2010, mostly in people having surgery, so general practice may differ. Specificity ranged from 10 to 100 across studies.
src: Cochrane review: physical examination for lumbar radiculopathy (2010)

murphy.scenario: Pain under the right ribs after a fatty meal. The doctor presses there and asks you to breathe in. If you stop mid-breath in pain, that’s positive.
murphy.says: Better at ruling in than out: it misses about 1 in 3. Hence the ultrasound.
murphy.note: Pooled figures from the Trowbridge 2003 JAMA review. Single studies varied a lot: 44 to 97 caught, 48 to 96 cleared.
src: Trowbridge 2003 JAMA review, teaching summary (University of Florida)

rovsing.scenario: Tummy pain that has moved to the lower right. The doctor presses on the lower left side. If it hurts on the right, that’s positive.
rovsing.says: A famous name doing modest work. It catches about 1 in 4 cases, so a negative barely matters.
rovsing.note: Pooled from studies of 902 children and adults in a 2022 review (Yale, Cureus). In pregnancy it caught 29 and cleared 64.

psoas.scenario: Lower-right tummy pain. You lie on your left side and the doctor gently pulls your right leg backwards. Tummy pain is positive.
psoas.says: Catches about 1 in 6. If it’s positive, appendicitis gets a bit more likely; if it’s negative, nothing much changes.
psoas.note: Pooled from studies of 1,187 children and adults in a 2022 review (Yale, Cureus).

homans.scenario: A sore, swollen calf after a long flight. The doctor bends your foot up towards your shin. Calf pain is positive.
homans.says: Old-school and unreliable: it shows up in anywhere from under 1 in 10 to about half of people with a clot. More than half of people without a clot have it too. Scores, D-dimer and ultrasound took over.
homans.note: No usable single figure for false alarms (only ‘more than half’), so one slider today. The grid shows the middle of the range.
src: GPnotebook: Homans’ sign (citing Joshua 2005, Intern Med J)

wells.scenario: A swollen calf. The doctor runs a checklist: recent surgery or bed rest? Cancer? Whole leg swollen? Is something else just as likely? The points add up to ‘likely’ or ‘unlikely’.
wells.says: Not meant to settle it alone. Its real trick is teamwork: in one big analysis, a low score plus a negative D-dimer left only about 1 in 100 with a clot.
wells.note: Spread across studies (GPnotebook, citing Stone 2017). The grid shows the middle of the range. Teamwork figure: 13 studies, about 10,000 people (NEJM Journal Watch summary).
src: GPnotebook: Wells score for DVT (citing Stone 2017)
NEJM Journal Watch: Wells rule plus D-dimer

phalen.scenario: Numb, tingly fingers that wake you at night. You press the backs of your hands together, wrists bent, for a minute. Tingling in the fingers is positive.
phalen.says: Middling both ways. A third of people with carpal tunnel pass it, and plenty without it fail. Nerve conduction studies are the usual tiebreaker.
phalen.note: A meta-analysis cited in J Fam Pract 2012 found 68 and 73; later meta-analyses landed nearby (57 to 69 caught, 67 to 71 cleared).
src: Wipperman and Potter 2012, Carpal tunnel syndrome: try these diagnostic maneuvers (J Fam Pract)

tinel.scenario: Same tingly fingers. The doctor taps over the front of your wrist. A zing shooting into the fingers is positive.
tinel.says: Tap, tap, coin toss. It catches half of cases. A JAMA review lumped Tinel’s and Phalen’s in with the least useful signs.
tinel.note: Figures from the table in a 2012 J Fam Pract review. The JAMA Rational Clinical Examination review (D’Arcy and McGee 2000) rated both as having little or no diagnostic value.
src: Wipperman and Potter 2012, Carpal tunnel syndrome: try these diagnostic maneuvers (J Fam Pract)

neer.scenario: Shoulder pain when you reach overhead. The doctor steadies your shoulder blade and lifts your straight arm up in front of you. Pain is positive.
neer.says: Good at catching it, bad at clearing it: about half of people without impingement say ouch anyway. Shoulders are complicated.
src: Hegedus 2008 meta-analysis (Br J Sports Med abstract)

hawkins.scenario: Same sore shoulder. The doctor lifts your arm to shoulder height, bends the elbow and swings the forearm down. Pain is positive.
hawkins.says: Neer’s near-twin, with the same problem: lots of false alarms.
src: Hegedus 2008 meta-analysis (Br J Sports Med abstract)

emptycan.condition: a full tear of a shoulder tendon (rotator cuff)
emptycan.scenario: A weak, painful shoulder. Arms out in front, thumbs down as if emptying a can, you push up while the doctor pushes down. Weakness or pain is positive.
emptycan.says: Studies can’t agree whether it’s brilliant or useless. Range scoring means almost anything wins today. Don’t get cocky.
emptycan.note: Hughes 2008 review: 32 to 99 caught, 40 to 91 cleared across studies. Single studies found 31/52 and 50/84. The grid shows the middle of the range.
src: Hughes 2008 systematic review, summarised by BestBETs

droparm.condition: a full tear of a shoulder tendon (rotator cuff)
droparm.scenario: The doctor lifts your arm out to the side, then asks you to lower it slowly. If it drops or you can’t control it, that’s positive.
droparm.says: Rarely positive, but when it is, take notice. It misses most tears.
droparm.note: Hughes 2008 review: 4 to 35 caught, 88 to 100 cleared across studies. The grid shows the middle of the range.
src: Hughes 2008 systematic review, summarised by BestBETs

dixhallpike.scenario: The room spins when you roll over in bed. The doctor turns your head and lies you back quickly, head tipped down, watching your eyes for a flicker.
dixhallpike.says: Good, not perfect: a negative doesn’t fully rule out BPPV. Bonus: a positive leads straight into the head-turning manoeuvre that treats it.
dixhallpike.note: Halker 2008 review. Few good studies, hence the very wide range for false alarms.

hints.scenario: Sudden nonstop spinning, vomiting, can’t walk straight. A doctor checks three things: a quick head turn, the pattern of eye flicker, and whether one eye sits higher.
hints.says: A few minutes of eye-watching catches almost all of these strokes. The catch is it needs trained eyes.
hints.note: Cochrane 2023, bedside HINTS in people with acute vertigo. About half the exams were done by neurologists. Low certainty.
src: Cochrane review: HINTS for acute vestibular syndrome (2023), abstract

drift.condition: a brain lesion weakening one side
drift.scenario: Arms straight out in front, palms up, eyes closed. If one arm slowly sinks and turns palm-in, that’s positive.
drift.says: A simple test that punches well above its weight: about 9 in 10 both ways.
drift.note: One study of 170 people with suspected mild one-sided brain lesions, checked against CT (Teitelbaum 2002).

shift.scenario: A swollen tummy. The doctor taps it like a drum, then rolls you onto your side and taps again to see whether the dull sound moves.
shift.says: Decent, not decisive. Ultrasound is the usual tiebreaker.
shift.note: Pooled figures from Williams and Simel 1992 (JAMA).
src: University of Washington Advanced Physical Diagnosis: ascites evidence
Veysey 2016, Detecting ascites (Med J Aust), from Williams and Simel 1992

wave.scenario: Another swollen tummy. Someone presses a hand down the middle while the doctor flicks one side and feels for a ripple on the other.
wave.says: Misses plenty, but when the ripple is there, it means business. Better for ruling in than out.
wave.note: Pooled figures from Williams and Simel 1992 (JAMA).
src: University of Washington Advanced Physical Diagnosis: ascites evidence
Veysey 2016, Detecting ascites (Med J Aust), from Williams and Simel 1992

jvp.scenario: Breathless in the emergency department. The doctor looks at a vein in your neck while you lie back at an angle, to see how high it fills.
jvp.says: If it’s up, heart failure gets much more likely. If it’s not, it tells you little: it missed 6 in 10.
jvp.note: Wang 2005 JAMA review of breathless adults in emergency departments.
src: Wang 2005 JAMA review, teaching summary (University of Florida)

s3.scenario: Same breathless patient. The doctor listens for an extra, low ‘gallop’ beat after the usual lub-dub.
s3.says: Rare, but rarely wrong. It caught about 1 in 8, yet a real S3 all but shouts the diagnosis. Hearing one takes a good ear and a quiet room.
s3.note: Wang 2005 JAMA review of breathless adults in emergency departments.
src: Wang 2005 JAMA review, teaching summary (University of Florida)

crt.scenario: A toddler with gastro. The doctor presses a fingertip until it goes pale and counts how long the pink takes to come back. Slow is positive.
crt.says: One of the most useful single signs, and it still misses about 4 in 10. Doctors combine several signs rather than trust one.
crt.note: Steiner 2004 JAMA review, for 5% dehydration or more. Few good studies, hence the wide ranges.
src: Steiner 2004 JAMA review, table reproduced in Evidencia (2008)
Steiner 2004 review, summarised in Evidence-Based Medicine (BMJ)

turgor.scenario: Same toddler. The doctor gently pinches the skin on the tummy and watches how fast it flattens back. Slow is positive.
turgor.says: A pinch that’s right more often than wrong, but not by much.
turgor.note: Steiner 2004 JAMA review, for 5% dehydration or more.
src: Steiner 2004 JAMA review, table reproduced in Evidencia (2008)
Steiner 2004 review, summarised in Evidence-Based Medicine (BMJ)

centor.scenario: Sore throat. The doctor ticks off four things: fever, swollen neck glands, pus on the tonsils, and no cough. Three or more counts as positive.
centor.says: Better than a guess, worse than a swab. It missed about 4 in 10 strep throats and flagged plenty of plain viral ones.
centor.note: Two reviews: the catching figure is from a 2023 review of hospital patients (medRxiv preprint); the clearing figure is from Aalbers 2011, adults in general practice.

ottawaknee.condition: a broken bone in the knee
ottawaknee.scenario: You landed hard on your knee. The doctor asks your age, presses the kneecap and the bony bump on the outside, then checks you can bend it and walk four steps. Any red flag means an X-ray.
ottawaknee.says: Just like its ankle cousin: it almost never misses a fracture, and about half of people without one still get sent for an X-ray. A fair trade.
src: Bachmann 2004 systematic review (Ann Intern Med abstract)

cspine.scenario: Rear-ended at the lights, neck sore. The doctor asks your age, how the crash happened and about any tingling, then checks whether you can turn your head. It decides who needs a scan.
cspine.says: Built to miss nothing, and it very nearly doesn’t. The price: more than half of people with no injury still get imaged.
cspine.note: Michaleff 2012 review (CMAJ), the 4 prospective studies that used the full rule. Across all 9 studies it caught 90 to 100 and cleared anywhere from 1 to 77.

fast.scenario: Someone suddenly can’t smile evenly. FAST checks the Face, both Arms and Speech, and if any is off, it’s Time to call 000.
fast.says: It misses about 1 in 4 strokes, which is why longer versions like BE-FAST add Balance and Eyes. If you see it, still call 000.
fast.note: Chen 2022 meta-analysis: 9 studies, 6,151 people, in ambulances, emergency departments and wards. Very mixed results for false alarms.
src: Chen 2022 meta-analysis, FAST vs BE-FAST (Frontiers in Neurology)

thompson.scenario: A loud snap at the back of your ankle during touch footy. You kneel on a chair and the doctor squeezes your calf. If your foot doesn’t point down, that’s positive.
thompson.says: A ten-second squeeze that almost never gets it wrong. Rare for a bedside test.
thompson.note: Reiman 2014 meta-analysis (J Athl Train), as reported by Physiotutors; FPnotebook gives the same figures.

trendel.condition: a gluteal tendon problem (outer hip pain)
trendel.scenario: Pain on the outside of your hip. You stand on the sore leg for half a minute. If the other side of your pelvis drops, that’s positive.
trendel.says: Respectable both ways, from one small study. Not bad for standing on one leg.
trendel.note: Bird 2001, checked against MRI in people with outer hip pain (summarised by BestBETs). Small study.
src: BestBETs: clinical tests for greater trochanteric pain

babinski.condition: damage to the brain or spinal cord’s movement wiring
babinski.scenario: The doctor strokes the sole of your foot with something blunt. If the big toe goes up instead of down, that’s positive. (In babies, up is normal.)
babinski.says: When it’s there, believe it. When it’s not, shrug: it missed about half.
babinski.note: A 2014 study of 107 adults seen by neurology, compared with a blinded expert diagnosis (J Neurol Sci).
src: Accuracy of the Babinski sign, 2014 (J Neurol Sci abstract)

papill.test: Eye check for a swollen optic nerve
papill.scenario: A child with worsening headaches. The doctor shines a light into the back of the eye to see whether the optic nerve looks swollen (papilloedema).
papill.says: No false alarms at all in this study, but it missed about half. A normal-looking eye doesn’t rule out raised pressure.
papill.note: One UK study of 60 children at a neurosurgical unit, checked against pressure monitoring (Childs Nerv Syst 2024). Small and specialised.
src: Papilloedema and raised intracranial pressure in children, 2024 (abstract)
